lead: Every file and directory on a Linux machine carries a permission mode, and that mode is written as ten characters in a long listing or as three or four octal digits on a command line. The mode answers one question: what may the owner, the group and everyone else do with this entry? It exists because Linux is multi-user, so one login must not silently rewrite another person's files. You use it every time you run chmod, every time umask decides the mode of a new file, and every time you wonder why a script will not run or a shared folder in /tmp is safe.
prereq: You need: the long listing from chapter 2.2 and some test files and directories from chapter 2.3.

blocks.text: In a long listing the first field is ten characters. Character 1 is the file type: - regular file, d directory, l symbolic link (see chapter 2.1). The other nine are three triads: owner (also called user), group, other. Other means everyone else on the machine. Inside a triad the order is always r, w, x. A letter allows the action, a dash refuses it. So -rwxr-xr-- reads as owner rwx, group r-x, other r--.
What r, w and x mean depends on whether the entry is a file or a directory.

On a directory, x is the right to traverse. To open /home/ravi/lab/report.txt the kernel walks /, /home, /home/ravi and lab, and each of those needs x for you. A directory with r but no x lists names, yet nothing inside can be opened. The x on a directory is not about running anything.

sections.h3: chmod in octal and in symbolic form

blocks.text: Each permission letter has a value: r = 4, w = 2, x = 1. Add the values inside one triad and you get a single octal digit 0 to 7. Three digits, one per triad, describe the whole mode.
chmod 754 notes.txt gives owner 4+2+1 = 7 (rwx), group 4+0+1 = 5 (r-x), other 4+0+0 = 4 (r--). The listing becomes -rwxr-xr--.

The symbolic form is chmod who op perms file. who is u (owner), g (group), o (other) or a (all three). op is + (add), - (remove) or = (set exactly). perms is any mix of r, w, x. Clauses are separated by commas.

items: chmod u+x,g+x,o-r notes.txt turns 644 into 750, the same as the octal command.
chmod go-w report.txt removes write from group and other.
chmod u=rwx,go=rx notes.txt sets 755 and clears anything not listed.
chmod -R 750 lab applies the mode to every entry below lab.

blocks.text: If you leave out who, the command is treated as a, but bits set in your umask are not touched, so chmod +x f can give 755 rather than 777.

New entries do not start at 777. The kernel starts from a base mode: 666 for a regular file (x is left out so that touch never hands you a runnable program) and 777 for a directory (without x you could not enter it). The umask holds the bits to remove, so 666 & ~umask and 777 & ~umask give the mode that is actually created.

umask with no argument prints the current value; umask 027 sets a new one for this shell and its children. With umask 022 a new file is 666 & ~022 = 644 (-rw-r--r--) and a new directory is 777 & ~022 = 755 (drwxr-xr-x).
Digit-wise subtraction from the base gives the same answer whenever each umask digit's bits fit inside the base digit, but writing it as 666 & ~umask is always correct.
A fourth octal digit sits in front of the nine and carries three special bits. Only a few syllabi teach these in this unit, so know what each one does and how it looks.

items: SUID (4): the program runs with the file owner's user id. /usr/bin/passwd needs it so an ordinary user can write /etc/shadow. The owner x slot shows s, or S when x is off.
SGID (2): the same idea for the group id on a program. On a directory it makes new files inherit the directory's group, which is how shared project folders work.

Sticky (1): on a directory, only the file's owner, the directory's owner or root may delete or rename an entry. /tmp is drwxrwxrwt, so everyone may write there and nobody may delete your file. The last slot shows t when x is also on, and T when the sticky bit is set but x is off.

blocks.text: chmod 1777 /tmp sets the sticky bit with open permissions.

examples.question: notes.txt shows -rw-r--r-- and is owned by ravi. (a) Give two commands, one octal and one symbolic, that change it to rwxr-x---. (b) With umask set to 022, what mode does touch a.txt give a new file, and what mode does mkdir d give a new directory? (c) A user with umask 022 wants new files to come out as 640 instead of 644. What must the umask be? (d) The directory lab is drwxr-x--- and the file lab/report.txt inside it is -rw-r--r--. priya is not ravi and is not in ravi's group. Can she read report.txt?
steps: (a) The current mode is 644. The target rwxr-x--- is 7, 5, 0, so the octal command is chmod 750 notes.txt.
Symbolic: owner 6 to 7 needs +x, group 4 to 5 needs +x, other 4 to 0 needs -r. Command: chmod u+x,g+x,o-r notes.txt.
(b) File base is 666, so 666 & ~022 = 644, that is -rw-r--r--. It has no x, because files never get x by default.
Directory base is 777, so 777 & ~022 = 755, that is drwxr-xr-x.
(c) Wanted 640 from base 666. Owner stays 6 (umask bit 0). Group 6 to 4 removes w, so umask digit 2. Other 6 to 0 removes r and w, so umask digit 4+2 = 6. The umask must be 026.
(d) For priya, both entries are checked in the other triad. lab is drwxr-x---, so other has ---, with no x. Without x she cannot traverse lab, so opening lab/report.txt fails with Permission denied.
The read bit on report.txt is never reached, because the kernel stops at the directory lookup.
examples.answer: (a) chmod 750 notes.txt or chmod u+x,g+x,o-r notes.txt; (b) new file 644, new directory 755; (c) umask 026; (d) no, she cannot read it because lab gives other no x.

traps: Other bits on a file are useless if a parent directory gives other no x. The kernel cannot reach the file to check its mode, and open fails with Permission denied.
The base mode for a file is 666, not 777. Subtracting the umask from 777 for a file gives a wrong answer, usually one with a phantom x.

A directory with mode 644 is broken for everyone, the owner included: there is no x in any triad, so nobody can enter it or create files inside it. The owner can only list the names (r), because w on a directory is useless without x.
With symbolic chmod, leaving out who makes the change respect your umask, so chmod +x f is not the same as chmod a+x f.
SUID is the lower-case s in the owner x slot. The upper-case S means the setuid bit is set but x is off, so the program cannot run and the bit does nothing.

quiz.q: Write the ten characters of a directory that the owner may read, write and enter, the group may read and enter, and others may not touch.
Give the octal value of r, w and x, and the mode string produced by chmod 640.
Why does x on a directory control access to the files inside it, even when those files are world-readable?
quiz.a: To open a file the kernel must resolve each path component in turn. Entering a directory component requires x on it. Without x the lookup stops there and the file's own mode is never examined, so open returns Permission denied.

quiz.q: A file is -rw-r--r--. Give two different commands that make it -rw-r-----, one octal and one symbolic.
quiz.a: chmod 640 file, or chmod o-r file. Both remove only the read bit from the other triad.

quiz.q: A shell has umask 027. What mode does touch f create, and what mode does mkdir d create? Give both in octal.
/tmp is drwxrwxrwt. Explain what each part of that mode allows and why the last bit is needed.
quiz.a: Everyone may list, create and traverse, so any program can use /tmp as scratch space. The t is the sticky bit: inside a directory with write and traverse for all, deletion is restricted to the owner of the file, the owner of the directory or root. Without it any user could delete another user's temporary file.

quiz.q: With umask 022, chmod +x script.sh gives 755 while chmod a+x script.sh gives 777 on a file that was 644. Explain the difference.
quiz.a: When who is omitted, the change is treated as a but bits set in the umask are protected. umask 022 protects group w and other w, so those stay off and only x is added to all three triads, giving 755. Naming a explicitly ignores the umask and adds x to all three triads of 644, giving 777.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real systems rarely stop at nine bits; POSIX ACLs add per-user and per-group entries through setfacl and getfacl, and that is where chapter 2.5 leads. Modern desktops and servers also carry mandatory access control modules such as SELinux and AppArmor, which decide access from a policy rather than from the mode. Linux capabilities split root's power into named rights such as CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE, so a program no longer needs to be setuid root. Containers reuse all of this: image layers store modes, and a careless chmod 777 in a Dockerfile is a common review comment. Search next for setfacl, getfacl, capabilities(7), and the find -perm option for auditing loose modes.
